archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (shot-volume, no finish)
archetype.definition: A winless Kings team that wins the shot and chance battle at 5-on-5 but has been buried by the league's worst finishing, near-worst goaltending and a broken penalty kill. The process looks like a middling team even though the results look like a lottery team.

report.headline: Six games, no wins, and a 92.8 PDO doing most of the damage
report.take:
Los Angeles is 0-4-2, 31st of 32 on the site, and has been outscored by 13 goals in six games. That is the worst start in the division by a distance. The 82-game pace reads 27 standings points, a number that tells you more about small samples than about this roster. Underneath the record is a team that has the puck. The Kings carry a 52% CF share (11th) and a 50.8% expected-goals share (15th), and they put 29.8 shots on goal a game, 8th in the league and well above the 27.2 league average. They allow 26.3, exactly league average. That is a profile of a middle-of-the-pack team, not a bottom-two one.

What has sunk them is everything that happens after the shot. Skaters are converting 6.7% of their shots, 31st and almost five points below the league's 11.3%. The goalies are stopping 86.1%, 30th, and the team's GSAx of -9 is 31st. Combined, that is an all-situations PDO of 92.8. Darcy Kuemper, with four of the six starts, sits at .847 and -5.3 GSAx, and that alone accounts for a large share of the gap. Special teams have piled on. A 61.9% penalty kill is 31st, and a 14.3% power play is 26th. A team out-chancing opponents at even strength cannot survive bleeding on the kill and failing to cash on the man advantage while also getting replacement-level saves.

The roster numbers show the split clearly. The top unit is driving play and getting punished for it. Artemi Panarin (60.9% xGF), Quinton Byfield (62.1%) and Adrian Kempe (59.6%) are all well above water in chances, yet they sit at -7, -6 and -5. Brandt Clarke posts a 72.4% xGF and five points from the blue line and is somehow -6. That is what bad on-ice shooting and saves look like. The real structural worry is the rest of the lineup. Moore, Haula and Laughton all sit near 41-43% xGF in middle-six minutes. Drew Doughty is at 39.6% in a team-high 20.34 minutes, and most of the blue line is under 46%. The D- forward grade and the F blue-line and goaltending grades are harsher than the shot shares, partly because the grades absorb these brutal results. Still, the depth problem is genuine.

History cuts both ways. Two seasons ago this was a 105-point team with the league's 2nd-best defense. Last year's 90 points came with a +5.6 points-over-goal-differential cushion and an offense ranked 29th. So the scoring issue is not new, and the penalty kill was already slipping at 74.6%. Expect the shooting and save percentages to climb and the losses to slow. What is less clear is whether this becomes a playoff team again or settles in as a bubble side that drove play and finished nothing.

strengths.title: Winning the shot and chance battle
strengths.body: The Kings out-attempt and slightly out-chance opponents at 5-on-5, and they generate more shots on goal than most of the league while allowing a league-average number. That is a repeatable, process-driven trait and the main reason to expect the record to improve. They also carried a CF share above 50% in each of the last two seasons, so this is part of their identity rather than a hot week.

strengths.title: Top line and Clarke driving play
strengths.body: Panarin, Byfield and Kempe each post expected-goal shares around 60% while playing over 21 minutes a night, and Brandt Clarke is at 72.4% with a team-high five points. Their ugly plus-minus figures reflect percentages, not how they are playing. When the shooting luck turns, this group is where the goals come from first.

concerns.title: Goaltending, Kuemper above all
concerns.body: The team's 86.1% save percentage and -9 GSAx are near the bottom of the league. Kuemper's .847 in four starts is the main culprit, and Forsberg has been less bad at .883 but still below expected. Some recovery is near certain because no goalie stays at .847. Still, if the crease only climbs to average, the Kings lose the edge their shot shares should give them.

concerns.title: A penalty kill in free fall
concerns.body: At 61.9%, the kill is 31st and 17 points below the league average. That is a gap no even-strength edge can cover. It was already a soft spot last season at 74.6%, so part of this is structural rather than pure noise, and goaltending on the kill is part of the same problem.

concerns.title: Finishing and thin depth
concerns.body: Skaters are shooting 6.7% against an 11.3% league norm. That will rise, but this offense also ranked 29th last year and the power play sits at 14.3%, so a finishing deficit is partly real. The middle six and most of the blue line are underwater in chances, which leaves the top unit carrying the whole load.

trend.note: After the 8-4 opener at Colorado, the defense tightened: goals allowed in the last five are 3.4 a game, better than the season rate. The offense has dried up to 1.6 a game, though, with four straight games scoring one goal.

weekAhead.headline: Five straight road games, three against elite goaltending
weekAhead.body:
This is a bad week for a team whose problem is finishing. Washington (A- goaltending, 7.4 GSAx), the Islanders (A goaltending, 10.4 GSAx, 1st) and the Rangers (A+ goaltending, 4th defense) all run high save percentages. All three are top-12 on the site. The Islanders and Rangers in particular choke off opposing forwards, ranking 3rd and 2nd at holding forwards under their expected points. The Kings' plan of piling up shots runs straight into goalies who have been stopping everything.

The softer spots come at either end of the back half. New Jersey is the league's best possession team (62% CF, 60.9% xGF) but has D- goaltending and a 69.6% penalty kill, so it should be a track meet. Chicago, 30th on the site, closes the week on the back end of a back-to-back. The Blackhawks are bottom-three in shot share and give up the second-most to defensemen, and it is the most winnable game on the trip. Realistically, one or two wins would count as progress.

keyMatchups.title: Kings shooters vs. Islanders, Rangers goalies
keyMatchups.body: The Islanders allow just 20.8 shots a game with a .940 save percentage, and the Rangers hold opposing wingers furthest under expectation in the league. For a team shooting 6.7%, these are the two games where regression is least likely to show up.

keyMatchups.title: Devils' leaky crease and kill
keyMatchups.body: New Jersey dominates possession but sits at an 86.9% save percentage and a 69.6% penalty kill. Expect the Kings to be out-shot. They still have a real chance to finally get goals, especially from the point, since the Devils give up the most to defensemen of any team.

keyMatchups.title: Chicago on the back-to-back
keyMatchups.body: The Blackhawks rank 29th in CF share and 30th in xGF share and allow 30.3 shots a game. That suits the Kings' volume game perfectly. If Los Angeles cannot win this one, the problem is bigger than percentages.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal and how many of the five Kuemper gets. A save percentage that climbs toward .890 would change this team's results faster than anything else.

restOfSeason.body:
The 0-4-2 start is mostly percentages. A 92.8 all-situations PDO built on 6.7% shooting and an .861 save percentage is not a level any team sustains. With shot shares above 50% and 76 games left, the Kings should play something close to .500 hockey or a bit better from here. The parts that look stickier are a scoring offense that was already 29th last season, a penalty kill that was below average a year ago, and depth forwards and defensemen who are losing their minutes. That points to a recovery into the bubble rather than back to the 105-point level of two seasons ago, roughly 78 to 90 points.

The ceiling depends on the crease. A Kuemper who returns to average turns many of these one-goal losses into points. If he stays near the bottom of the goalie tab, the six-game hole and a weak Pacific bottom half will leave Los Angeles chasing all year.
swingFactors: Penalty kill climbing back toward league average
Depth lines holding their own in chance share

confidence.note: Six games, with the record driven by extreme shooting and save percentages that will move.
